name: Diego Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a motor claims handler at a car insurer's claims centre, on the second floor of an office park out by the ring road. I log on at eight, and the first hour is new claims from overnight: rear-end bumps, cracked windscreens, the odd car that's been stolen from a driveway. I check the policy covers it, order the garage estimate, and decide whether it's a repair or a write-off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzles, honestly. When two drivers tell completely different stories about the same roundabout, and you piece it together from dashcam clips and photos, that's satisfying. What wears me out is the chasing: garages that don't send invoices, customers who ring four times a day because their courtesy car is late.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, I rent a flat with my partner Ana, who's a physiotherapist at a sports clinic. No kids yet. We've got about four months of costs put away. I did a two-year college diploma in business admin, and I've been at the claims centre five years now. I use the AI tools there every day, more than most people on my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so, a bit. Everyone at the claims centre got excited when the photo-damage tool came in, and I'd say it's a good helper but it was never going to replace us. Online I'd just post something dry about the hype being over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a little disappointed. I've put real time into learning these tools, and I was hoping that would set me apart. If it all stays small, I'm back to being one good handler among forty, and the way up is the slow way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and push for the team lead role when Joanna moves on, probably in the next year or two. I'd keep using the tools for summaries and letters because they save me maybe an hour a day. Ana and I would keep saving for a deposit, about 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit flat, if I'm honest, like a film that promised a big ending and just stopped. But the job's fine and the money's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools save you an hour a day. What happens to that hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now it goes on the hard claims, the disputed ones. In this picture the company would notice the hour, though, and quietly give each of us more claims. That's already happening a little. I've gone from about sixty open files to seventy-five in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your own life that would still worry you here, even with AI staying small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mainly. Our landlord put it up nine percent last spring, and if he does that again we'll be looking at smaller places further out. That's a bigger threat to my year than any chatbot. In this picture, the rent hikes are the real story and AI is just a footnote.

say: I'd say the photo-damage tool is a **good helper**, but it was never going to replace claims handlers.
I'd post something dry online about the **hype** finally being over.
think: I'd feel a bit **let down**, because my time learning the tools would matter less.
I'd be one good handler among forty again, with only the **slow way** up.
do: Go for the **team lead** role when Joanna moves on in a year or two.
Keep using AI for **summaries and letters**, saving about an hour a day.
Keep saving about **300 a month** with Ana for a house deposit.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a flat feeling, like a film that promised a big ending.
The **rent rises** worry me more than anything AI does here.
S0.quote: In this picture, the rent hikes are the real story and AI is just a footnote.
fieldNote: He is an early adopter who would feel **cheated of an edge** if AI stalled.
Rising **rent** is his real pressure, and he names it unprompted.
He already notices the **saved hour** turning into a bigger caseload, from sixty to seventy-five files.

steps.text: Apply for the team lead role at the claims centre when it opens
Put 300 a month into the joint house deposit account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like the last one, I'll read it and then ask the same questions. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance, and I'd mean it. I'd be the one telling the team that the people who learn to check the AI's work will be the ones still here. Online I'd probably share the odd tip about prompts for claims letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think motor claims is right in the firing line. Checking cover, ordering estimates, writing to customers, all of it is thinking work the card lists. The insurer won't fire forty people on a Monday. The insurer will just stop replacing the ones who leave, and in three years the team is twenty-five. I'd better be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Joanna to put me on the pilot group for whatever claims software comes next, this month, not later. I'd do an online course in claims data, the kind that teaches you to spot where the AI gets it wrong. And I'd build our savings from four months to six, in case I guess wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's some excitement in it too. I'd rather be inside the change than waiting for it to land on me. It's the colleagues who hate computers that I'd lie awake about, more than myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, mainly. He's been handling claims for twenty years and he still prints every file. He's brilliant on the phone with upset customers, but he's said out loud he'll never touch the AI tools. In this picture he's the first one they'd let go, and he's got a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they'd stop replacing people. How sure are you that you'd be one who stays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly sure, maybe seven out of ten. I'm good with the tools and I'm cheap compared to the seniors. But I'm average on the actual claims judgment, and if the software gets that part right too, being keen won't save me. That's the gap I'd work on.

say: I'd tell the team this is our **chance** to move into checking the AI's work.
I'd share **prompt tips** for claims letters online, keeping it practical rather than preachy.
think: Motor claims sits right in the **firing line**, because nearly every task is on the card.
The team would shrink by **not replacing leavers**, maybe from forty to twenty-five.
do: Ask to join the **pilot group** for new claims software this month.
Take an online course in **claims data** and spotting AI errors.
Build savings from four months to **six months** of costs.
feel: **Uneasy**, but partly excited to be inside the change.
I'd **worry more** about older colleagues like Gary than about myself.
S1.quote: The insurer won't fire forty people on a Monday. The insurer will just stop replacing the ones who leave, and in three years the team is twenty-five.
fieldNote: He describes a **quiet shrink** through leavers not replaced, rather than layoffs.
His confidence is **seven out of ten**, and he admits his claims judgment is only average.
Concern for **Gary**, a twenty-year colleague with a mortgage, came up before his own risks.

steps.text: Ask Joanna for a place on the claims software pilot group
Finish an online course on claims data and AI errors
Grow savings from four to six months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone would say: that it's huge, and we need to work out what claims handling even is now. At work I'd try to sound steady for the younger ones. Online, honestly, I'd probably go quiet and just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is gone. If AI can do almost any thinking work by 2028, then a claims desk is one of the first things they switch over, because it's all screens and rules. Being good with the AI tools only buys me a few months, not a career, when the whole claims desk is screens and rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd look hard at becoming a motor engineer, the people who go out and inspect damaged cars in person. That's hands-on, so it might give me until about 2031. I'd ask the insurer if they'd fund the assessor qualification, and I'd stop the house deposit and keep that money as a cushion instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops a bit just saying it. Two years isn't long enough to become someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ana actually talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whose job carries us. Ana's a physio, so her work is hands-on, and she'd likely keep going a few years longer than me. I'd probably say, half joking, that I'm going to be the house husband. She'd say not a chance, go and learn something with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the motor engineer route buys three years. Then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I honestly don't know. Three years of inspecting bent cars, and then the robots can do that too. I suppose by then everything has changed so much that the plan isn't really about a job anymore. It's about whatever the government and the companies decide to do with everyone.

say: I'd say it's **huge**, and we'd have to rethink what claims handling even is.
I'd try to sound **steady** at work for the younger handlers, then go quiet online.
think: My claims desk job is **gone**, because it's all screens and rules.
Being good with the tools only **buys months**, not a career.
do: Look into training as a **motor engineer** who inspects damaged cars in person.
Ask the insurer to fund the **assessor qualification** before 2028.
Pause the **house deposit** and keep that money as a cushion.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a drop in my stomach just saying it.
Two years feels **too short** to become someone else.
S2.quote: Being good with the AI tools only buys me a few months, not a career, when the whole claims desk is screens and rules.
fieldNote: His early-adopter edge **disappears** in his own reckoning once AGI arrives in two years.
He sees the hands-on **motor engineer** route as a three-year bridge, not an answer.
Ana's **hands-on job** as a physio becomes the household's main anchor.

steps.text: Ask the insurer to fund a motor engineer assessor qualification
Keep the house deposit savings as an emergency cushion instead
Put the plan to buy a house with Ana on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them. At work I'd push for the company to run a proper retraining plan instead of drip-feeding redundancies. Online I'd share what I was learning, as I went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to change direction, if I start straight away. The desk job still ends around 2031. But I can be somewhere else by then, and I'd rather pick where than be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the motor engineer course at evening college, and get some weekends shadowing at a body shop my cousin works at. I'd stay at the claims centre and keep getting paid while I learn. We'd still save for a house, just smaller, maybe 200 a month instead of 300.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way, not a frozen way. Having a list helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather pick where. What would picking look like by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where I'm physically in front of the car, the customer and the damage. Maybe an engineer for a fleet company, checking delivery vans after accidents. The robots come around 2034 in this picture, so that's three more years on top, and by then I'd want a second skill too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the company owes the people on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honest notice, mainly. Tell us in 2027 what the claims centre will look like in 2031. I don't think the insurer owes anyone a job forever, but it does owe us the truth early enough to act on it.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so we should use them properly.
I'd push the company for a **retraining plan** instead of drip-fed redundancies.
think: Five years is enough to **change direction** if I start immediately.
My desk job still **ends around 2031**, so I'd rather choose than be pushed.
do: Take the **motor engineer course** at evening college in year one.
Shadow at my cousin's **body shop** on weekends while still earning.
Cut the deposit savings from 300 to **200 a month**.
feel: **Anxious**, but busy rather than frozen, because having a list helps.
S3.quote: I don't think the insurer owes anyone a job forever, but it does owe us the truth early enough to act on it.
fieldNote: He treats five years as **workable**, and plans to keep earning while he retrains.
His fairness line is **honest notice**, not job guarantees, which fits his centre views.
He already thinks past 2034 and wants a **second skill**.

steps.text: Enrol in the motor engineer evening course at the local college
Push with colleagues for a company retraining plan for the claims team
Keep saving 200 a month toward a smaller house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real gift, and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. At work I'd say the claims centre should start moving people now. Online I'd be more upbeat than most, because I like this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine in this one. I'll be 37 in 2036. That's enough time to do a proper second career and maybe even a degree, while the claims job pays the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next two years getting really good at the claims software, maybe moving into the team that sets it up. Then I'd start a part-time degree in automotive engineering around 2028. We'd still buy a flat, probably in 2028, because Ana's job is steady and we'd know what we're facing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. It's on my mind, but I feel like I'm holding the steering wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd set up the claims software. Doesn't that speed up the end of your own team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I've thought about that. If I don't do it, someone in another office will, and the team shrinks anyway. At least from inside I can tell them which bits still need a person, like the calls with someone whose car was just stolen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self, starting at the claims centre at 22?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the cars, not just the paperwork. I spent five years getting fast at insurance forms. The forms are what disappear first, and the car is still sitting in the car park. Someone still has to go and look at it.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real gift**, and wasting it would be on us.
I'd sound more **upbeat** than most people, because I like this technology.
think: I'd be **fine** in this one, because I'm only 37 in 2036.
There's time for a proper **second career** while the claims job pays.
do: Move into the team that **sets up** the claims software within two years.
Start a part-time **automotive engineering** degree around 2028.
Buy a **flat** with Ana around 2028, since her work is steady.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, like I'm still holding the steering wheel.
S4.quote: I spent five years getting fast at insurance forms. The forms are what disappear first, and the car is still sitting in the car park.
fieldNote: With ten years he expects to land **on his feet** and plans in phases.
He accepts that setting up the software **speeds the shrink** of his own team.
His key lesson is to **learn the cars**, not the paperwork.

steps.text: Apply to join the team that configures the claims software
Start a part-time automotive engineering degree around 2028
Buy a flat with Ana around 2028

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. Two years is the problem, not the AI. What would help is if insurers had to give real notice and fund training before they switch a team over, like a year's warning and a course paid for. Even a bridging payment for people retraining into hands-on work would change everything for someone like Gary.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's actually going to check the AI's decisions. Somebody will get a claim refused by a machine and have nobody to ring. I'd happily do that job, the human at the end of the line, if anyone decides it's worth paying for.

headlineQuote: Somebody will get a claim refused by a machine and have nobody to ring.
portrait: Diego is a 27-year-old **motor claims handler** who uses AI tools daily and rents a flat with Ana, a physiotherapist.
He expects claims desks to **shrink through leavers** not being replaced, and gives himself seven-in-ten odds of staying.
With AGI in two years he sees his job as **gone** and eyes motor engineering as a bridge.
With five or ten years he becomes **confident**, planning evening courses, a degree and a flat purchase.
He blames no one in particular, but wants **honest notice** from employers rather than promises.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain into hands-on work.
whatWouldHelp: A **year's notice** and paid training before insurers switch a team over to AI.
A **bridging payment** for clerks retraining into hands-on jobs.
